extracted.intended_audience: university mathematics instructors, mathematics education researchers, and assessment designers
extracted.subtask_description: Designing and evaluating criterion-referenced (standards-based) assessment for undergraduate mathematics courses, including how to construct and present criteria/standards, align tasks to learning outcomes, and measure student perceptions. Also covers related teacher-knowledge criteria (knowledge at the mathematical horizon) and instructional design for reinvention of formal definitions in calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion-referenced assessment (CRA) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Assessment based on pre-determined and clearly articulated criteria and associated standards of knowledge, skills, competencies and/or capabilities; determines the extent to which a learner achieves certain predetermined goals without reference to the performance of others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: CRA contrasts with norm-referenced approaches; it requires explicit statements of what is to be achieved and uses those standards to judge performance rather than comparing students to each other (cites Brown 1988; Harvey 2004; TEDI 2006).

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation components of CRA
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing CRA involves: (a) designing or stating a set of learning outcomes for a course; (b) designing an assessment program to obtain information about a student's performance in relation to those outcomes; and (c) presenting a criteria set and definition of standards to both inform students how their performance will be judged and to provide directions for assessors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These three components should be explicitly documented and communicated. The criteria/standards serve both formative (guide learning) and summative (grade allocation) roles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link subtasks of assessment to learning outcomes (constructive alignment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subtasks of assessment activities should be explicitly linked with the learning outcomes of the course (e.g., knowledge, insight, understanding, skills) so that assessment functions as an educational tool rather than mere reproduction of facts or algorithms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This promotes 'constructive alignment' (Biggs, 1996) by aligning content, pedagogy and assessment. The paper argues this makes assessment more useful for learning than traditional right/wrong marking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present criteria and standards to students with grading translation
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide students with a set of criteria and standard definitions in addition to the actual problems; give details of exactly how responses to the mathematical problems will be graded and how translation between the mathematics and the standards and criteria will be carried out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students should receive the grading rubric (criteria + standards) prior to attempting tasks so they understand how marks will be allocated and what constitutes different standards of performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Go beyond simple right/wrong criteria while maintaining mathematical integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: CRA in quantitative courses should extend beyond binary 'right-or-wrong' judgments to capture dimensions like understanding, insight, and skills, yet preserve mathematical rigor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The experiment demonstrates it is possible to implement richer criterion-referenced grading for mathematics tasks without compromising mathematical correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit guidance to students and graders about use of criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Students and graders need explicit instruction about why criteria are provided, how criteria can be used to assist learning (e.g., guiding responses), and how to use criteria to interpret feedback post-grading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors recommend demonstrating to students 'what the grader will deem to be important' and training graders in using the criteria so feedback is meaningful. Evidence from the study: students found criteria understandable and useful for clarifying scoring but often did not use them to approach tasks unless guided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Careful construction and faculty guidance in developing criteria/standards
rubrics_metrics.description: The construction of criteria and standards is not straightforward; academic staff need close guidance in developing these elements of a CRA strategy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Developing valid, reliable criteria requires effort and support – it is the kind of judgement normally made implicitly and thus needs explicit attention and training for staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain course assessment structure while implementing CRA (procedural constraint)
rubrics_metrics.description: When introducing CRA, it's possible to keep the existing assessment program structure (e.g., progressive non-exam assessment contributing 40% and mid/ final exams 60%) while implementing criterion-referenced grading for certain tasks (assignments).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reported experiment preserved prior weightings but replaced assignment marking with explicit criteria and standards to test CRA impact without overhauling the whole assessment scheme.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-perceived comprehensibility and usefulness of criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate CRA by measuring whether students find the assessment criteria easy to understand and useful in informing how they will be graded, and whether the criteria help them re-interpret feedback.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the study, quantitative Likert data indicated students found criteria understandable and useful for understanding grading; qualitative data showed many students did not use criteria to change how they approached tasks, though some consulted criteria after grading to interpret errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria improve clarity of score allocation
rubrics_metrics.description: One purpose/metric of CRA is that the criteria make the process of allocating scores by graders much clearer to students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students reported CRA clarified how graders allocated marks; this transparency is an intended benefit and a success metric for CRA.

rubrics_metrics.name: Horizon knowledge (KMH) definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Horizon knowledge is an awareness of how mathematical topics are related across the curriculum and an appreciation of the larger mathematical landscape in which current instruction is situated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Described as an 'experienced and appreciative tourist' perspective that illuminates connections not necessarily in the immediate curriculum but useful for student learning (Ball & Bass, 2009).

rubrics_metrics.name: Elements of knowledge at the mathematical horizon
rubrics_metrics.description: Horizon knowledge consists of four elements: (1) a sense of the mathematical environment surrounding the current 'location' in instruction; (2) major disciplinary ideas and structures; (3) key mathematical practices; and (4) core mathematical values and sensibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These four elements provide a rubric for what counts as useful 'horizon' content teachers can draw on to enrich instruction and orient students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inner vs outer horizon distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Inner horizon: features of a mathematical object not at the focus of attention but that surround its current location (e.g., disciplinary ideas and structures). Outer horizon: features not part of the object but connected to the world in which the object exists (e.g., practices, values, sensibilities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This philosophical framing (from Husserl) helps distinguish types of KMH teachers might access: inner (theory/structure) vs outer (applications/values).

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of advanced mathematical knowledge (AMK) as KMH
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers' advanced mathematical knowledge (AMK) can instantiate KMH when it is applied to elementary/secondary curriculum topics to illuminate structure, resolve student confusion, or make connections (e.g., group theory ideas to clarify inverse notation; calculus insights to explain derivative–area relations).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Miss Scarlett, Mrs. Peacock) illustrate effective uses: applying group theory to distinguish inverse vs reciprocal; using geometric intuition from calculus to link derivatives of area/volume to perimeter/surface area. The rubric values flexibility, accessibility, and student-resonant application of AMK.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guided reinvention instructional design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Instructional activities should (a) link up with students' informal situated knowledge, (b) enable development of more sophisticated, abstract, formal knowledge, and (c) comply with the principle of intellectual autonomy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the guided reinvention heuristic (Gravemeijer) used to support students in formalizing informal intuitions; it serves as criteria for designing tasks that lead to student-generated formal definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional methods to support reinvention of formal definitions
rubrics_metrics.description: Use graphical representations and unpacking of convergent series, prompt students to generate definitions by completing stems (e.g., 'A series converges when...'), use iterative refinement and unpacking of elements within definitions, and employ contextualized examples (e.g., Taylor polynomials and focusing on particular x-values/vertical number lines for pointwise convergence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The teaching experiment comprised multiple sessions with iterative refinement; tasks were inspired by proofs-and-refutations heuristics (Lakatos) and designed to move students from informal to formal epsilon-N definitions via concrete visualizations and dialogic prompting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence/criteria of successful reinvention
rubrics_metrics.description: Successful reinvention is indicated by students producing rigorous formal definitions (e.g., epsilon-N definition of series convergence), unpacking the meaning of elements within those definitions, and using those definitions to reason about related concepts (e.g., pointwise convergence of Taylor series).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The paper focuses on the evolution of student definitions across sessions and treats the ability to articulate and unpack formal definitions as the key success metric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of proofs-and-refutations (Lakatos) heuristic in task design
rubrics_metrics.description: Design activities using the proofs-and-refutations approach to stimulate historical-style mathematical discovery and iterative refinement of definitions/theorems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors adapted Larsen & Zandieh's (2007) adaptation of Lakatos to structure tasks that encourage students to conjecture, find counterexamples, and refine definitions—criterion for pedagogical design in reinvention experiments.
